65-001.r: Dharwar system → India's most mineralised rock system and main source of metallic minerals: high-grade iron ore, manganese, copper, lead, gold.

65-003.r: Chhotanagpur plateau → 'storehouse of Indian minerals'; for its mineral wealth also called the 'Ruhr of India'.

65-004.r: Vindhyan rocks → sedimentary; rich in limestone (base of the cement industry), sand and china clay.

65-005.r: Odisha → largest iron-ore producer in 2023-24; India's iron-ore output that year (P) about 277.33 million tonnes.

65-006.r: Largest mineral reserves → south-east to north-east belt of the peninsula (Chota Nagpur, Dandakaranya, Odisha plateaus): coal, iron, mica, copper, bauxite; 'heart of Indian minerals'.

65-007.r: Mineral value 2024-25: Odisha 43.49% > Rajasthan 16.26% > Chhattisgarh 13.69% > Karnataka 12.42% > Maharashtra 4.76%; 8 states give about 97.70%. Among options, Karnataka.

65-008.r: Bihar (then including Jharkhand) was richest in minerals when asked. Now, by value (2024-25): Odisha > Rajasthan > Chhattisgarh > Karnataka > Maharashtra > Jharkhand.

65-009.r: Odisha → 'State of Minerals': coal, iron ore, bauxite, chromite; some of India's largest bauxite and chromite deposits.

65-010.r: Gondwana rocks → about 99.54% of India's coal (A true); Dharwar rocks → most ferrous and non-ferrous minerals (R true); but R doesn't explain A.
65-010.c: The book places the Damodar Basin coalfields (Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro) in Odisha; they lie in Jharkhand and West Bengal.

65-011.r: Marble → non-metallic mineral; manganese, silver, lead are metallic. India produces 95 minerals: 4 fuel, 10 metallic, 23 non-metallic, 3 atomic, 55 minor.

66-001.r: Iron ore in India → mainly in the Dharwar rock system, the most economically valuable rock system.

66-004.r: Iron ore output 2023-24 (P): Odisha 148.96 mt (53.71%) > Chhattisgarh 46.03 (16.60%) > Karnataka 40.99 (14.78%) > Jharkhand 22.89. Top two then and now: Odisha, Chhattisgarh.
66-004.c: Chhattisgarh, not Karnataka, ranked second in the year the question refers to as well as in the book's 2023-24 data (16.60% vs 14.78%), so (a) Odisha and Chhattisgarh is the right answer.

66-005.r: Iron ore resources (IMYB 2024, thousand t): Odisha 9409573, Madhya Pradesh 356999, Bihar 49494. Haematite: Odisha 39%, Jharkhand 19.58%, Chhattisgarh 19.09%, Karnataka 11.79%.
66-005.c: Today's data favour (b): Madhya Pradesh holds far more iron ore than Bihar (356999 vs 49494 thousand tonnes). The printed (c) reflects old undivided Bihar, which included Jharkhand's rich deposits.

66-006.r: Iron-ore areas: Kudremukh (Karnataka, mostly magnetite) and Singhbhum (now West Singhbhum) → two options fit, so the book gives no single answer (*).

66-007.r: Punjab → no iron ore. Regions: North-East (Jharkhand, Odisha), Central (Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Maharashtra), Peninsular (Karnataka, Goa, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala); Bihar then included Jharkhand.

66-009.r: Mineral–country: Silver → Mexico; Mica → India; Iron ore → Russian Federation; Copper → Chile.

66-010.r: Bailadila (Dantewada, Chhattisgarh) → haematite. Haematite: Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Goa; higher-grade magnetite: Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Goa.
66-010.t: Don't confuse: Bailadila ore is haematite; magnetite has more iron and is found mainly in Karnataka.

66-011.r: Iron mines: Gurumahisani → Odisha (Mayurbhanj); Bailadila → Chhattisgarh (Dantewada); Noamundi → Jharkhand (West Singhbhum); Kudremukh → Karnataka (Chikkamagaluru).

66-013.r: Bailadila (Dantewada, Chhattisgarh) → India's largest mechanised mine; linked to the Vizag steel plant, Visakhapatnam; iron ore exported to Japan.

66-014.r: Bailadila → Chhattisgarh; Kendujhar → Odisha; Balaghat → Madhya Pradesh; Kudremukh → Karnataka.

66-015.r: Richest (magnetite) iron-ore reserves → Karnataka; largest producer → Odisha; India is 3rd, not 2nd, in world iron-ore output (2023) → statements 1 and 3.

66-016.r: Iron ore reserves (haematite + magnetite, 1-4-2020, IMYB 2024), among options: Karnataka > Odisha > Jharkhand > Chhattisgarh.

66-017.r: Wrong pair: Iron ore–Guntur. Correct: Gold–Kolar, Coal–Jharia, Diamonds–Panna.

66-018.r: Haematite → largest iron-ore reserve type in India: about 24057905 thousand tonnes (1 April 2020, IMYB 2024).

66-019.r: Iron ores: limonite [FeO(OH)·nH2O], haematite, magnetite, siderite. Cinnabar → mercury; bauxite → aluminium; pyrite (FeS2) is used for sulphuric acid, not iron extraction.

66-021.r: Chiria (West Singhbhum, Jharkhand) → famous for iron ore mining.

66-022.r: Wrong statement: 80% of iron-ore reserves in Jharkhand and Odisha; haematite there is only 58.58% (Odisha 39%, Jharkhand 19.58%). Magnetite: Karnataka 69.50%. Bellary, Mayurbhanj statements true.

67-001.r: Rampur Agucha (Bhilwara) → Asia's best zinc-lead reserves. Rajasthan has a near monopoly in zinc and lead (2023-24); other deposits: Zawar (Udaipur), Dungarpur, Alwar.

67-002.r: Rajasthan → near monopoly in zinc; holds 89.32% of India's lead-zinc ore reserves (1 April 2020, IMYB 2024).

68-001.r: Silver not found in Gujarat. Silver reserves (1 April 2020): 30267.91 t metal; Rajasthan 86.29%, Karnataka 4.56%, Jharkhand 4.19%, Andhra Pradesh 2.98%; Odisha also has some.

69-001.r: Malajkhand (Balaghat, MP) → copper. Madhya Pradesh → largest copper ore producer. Key copper districts: Jhunjhunu (Rajasthan), Balaghat (MP), East Singhbhum (Jharkhand).

69-004.r: Malanjkhand (Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh) → open-pit copper mine; Madhya Pradesh is the leading copper ore producer (IMYB 2024).

69-005.r: Largest copper ore reserves → Rajasthan (1 April 2020, IMYB 2024).

69-006.r: Copper fields: Chandrapur → Maharashtra; Hassan → Karnataka; Khammam → Andhra Pradesh (now Telangana); Khetri → Rajasthan.

69-007.r: Map question: copper deposit found in 1999 by the Atomic Minerals Cell → area 4, southern Karnataka.

69-008.r: Khetri (Jhunjhunu district, Rajasthan) → famous for copper.

69-009.r: Khetri belt (Jhunjhunu district, Rajasthan) → copper mining.

70-001.r: Bauxite → ore of aluminium; white, pink or red by iron content. Top producers (IMYB 2024): Odisha, Jharkhand, Gujarat.

70-002.r: Bauxite (Ministry of Mines report 2020-21): Odisha 1st, Gujarat 2nd, Chhattisgarh 3rd → Odisha and Gujarat. IMYB 2024: Odisha, then Jharkhand.

70-003.r: Bauxite (15–25% aluminium) → only ore used commercially for aluminium. Odisha → largest producer: Kalahandi, Koraput, Sundargarh, Bolangir, Sambalpur.

70-004.r: Bauxite leaders: Gujarat and Odisha when asked (b); 2023-24 (P): Odisha > Jharkhand > Gujarat > Maharashtra > Chhattisgarh. The book gives no single answer (*).

70-005.r: Kalahandi → bauxite; Zawar → zinc and lead; Kolar → gold; Mosabani → copper.

70-006.r: Bauxite in Chhattisgarh → Kabirdham, Kondagaon and Surguja districts.

70-007.r: Bauxite resources (1.4.2020): Odisha 41.49% > Chhattisgarh 20% > Andhra Pradesh 12% > Gujarat 8% > Jharkhand 6%.

71-001.r: Chhattisgarh → only tin-producing state, immense tin ore deposits. Tin ore resources (1/04/2020): Haryana 64.39%, Chhattisgarh 35.59%.

71-002.r: Tin → Chhattisgarh is the only tin-producing state in India (2023-24, P).

71-003.r: Chhattisgarh's notable reserve → tin ore; per IMYB 2024 it holds India's second-largest tin ore reserves.

72-001.r: Mica producer: Andhra Pradesh when asked (a); Rajasthan is the biggest producer now (2021-22, IMYB 2022). The book gives no single answer (*).

72-002.r: Largest producers: bauxite → Odisha (2021-22); mica → Rajasthan (IMYB 2022). No option matches; RPSC dropped the question. Mica declared a minor mineral, 10 February 2015.

72-004.r: Mica reserves (1/4/2015, IMYB 2021): Andhra Pradesh 41%, Rajasthan 28%, Odisha 17%, Bihar 2% → Rajasthan, as Andhra Pradesh isn't an option.

72-005.r: Mica: Madhya Pradesh didn't produce it when asked (b). 2021-22: Rajasthan the only producer. Reserves: Andhra Pradesh 41%, Rajasthan 28%, Odisha 17%, Maharashtra 13%, Bihar 2%.

72-006.r: Largest mica belt → Hazaribagh, Gaya, Munger and Koderma ('Capital of Mica'); mica occurs in veins of metamorphic rocks.

72-007.r: Map question: the black marks show the distribution of mica.

72-008.r: In 2001 India led world sheet-mica production. Now (2022): China 1st, Madagascar 2nd in mica.

72-009.r: World leaders (2022): mica → China; copper → Chile; gypsum → USA; iron ore → Australia. India leads none → (e).

73-001.r: Best marble → Makrana (Rajasthan); Taj Mahal and Victoria Memorial (Kolkata) are built of Makrana marble.
73-001.c: Makrana is not in 'Nagpur district': it was in Nagaur district of Rajasthan and now lies in the new Didwana-Kuchaman district carved out of Nagaur.

73-002.r: Marble → metamorphic rock, formed when limestone undergoes heat and pressure.

73-003.r: Marble → recrystallised limestone (recrystallised carbonate minerals); a metamorphic rock.

74-001.r: India's first coal mine → Raniganj, on the Damodar river, mined from 1774.

74-002.r: Coal timeline: Raniganj first production 1774 (Sumner and Heatly, East India Company) → NCDC 1956 → nationalisation (coking 1971-72, non-coking 1973) → Coal India Ltd.

74-003.r: Map question: Karanpura coalfield is wrongly placed; it lies in Jharkhand. Satpura, Son Valley and Korba are shown about right.

74-004.r: Gondwana system → main source of India's coal: over 99% of deposits and production; mostly eastern and central peninsula, also Assam and Sikkim.

74-007.r: Indian coal → high ash content, low sulphur (1 and 2). Over 99% from Gondwana coal; Kalp-region coal is inferior and sulphur-rich. Gondwana rocks hold over 90% of reserves.
74-007.c: The explanation says Gondwana coal has little ash, but the book's answer (a) rightly treats Indian coal as high-ash.

74-009.r: Self-sufficient for three decades → coking coal (coal reserves last ~80 years vs petroleum 22, gas 30). Coal resources: 400.715 billion t (1 April 2025); coking coal 6.35% of output.

74-010.r: Coal resources 400.715 billion t (1 April 2025), not 293.50 → A false today; more than half proved reserves in Jharkhand and Odisha → R true (d). Commission took (b).
74-010.c: The book concludes (d): coal resources are now 400.715 billion tonnes, so A's 293.50 is outdated. Option (b) is misprinted (it should say 'not the correct explanation'); that was the commission's key.

74-011.r: Coal reserves: Odisha 100.99 billion t and Jharkhand 93.25 billion t → together over 50%; then West Bengal 34.39.

74-012.r: Both true: India 2nd in world coal output 2023 (11.11%) after China (51.78%), then Indonesia 8.52%, USA 5.77%; big reserves in Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh.

74-013.r: Coal output in 1999: undivided Bihar (with Jharkhand) > undivided Madhya Pradesh (with Chhattisgarh) > West Bengal. 2024-25: Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh.

74-014.r: Two leading coal producers (2024-25, Ministry of Coal) → Odisha and Jharkhand.

74-015.r: Coal output 2007-08 (when asked): Jharkhand > Chhattisgarh > Odisha > Madhya Pradesh. 2024-25: Odisha > Jharkhand > Chhattisgarh > Madhya Pradesh > Telangana. Coal = 'Black Diamond'.

74-016.r: Largest coal producer (2024-25) → Odisha (about 25.71%), followed by Jharkhand.

74-018.r: Proved coal reserves (1 April 2023): Odisha > Jharkhand > Chhattisgarh > West Bengal > Madhya Pradesh → no option matches; the book gives no single answer (*).
